Kielbasa Stew is my all time favorite dinner. It's cheap and easy to prepare, freezes well and feels like good hearty man food.

Chop up some taters into large chunks and start 'em boiling. I like to keep mine in good size pieces, no smaller than 1" on any side. Be aware of how much water they're boiling in, as you won't be draining them.

Get a big horseshoe of kielbasa sausage and chop it up as well, slit each piece of sausage lengthwise so it can open up and release all those wonderful sausage fats and spices into the pot.

Add equal size chunks of carrot shortly after the potatoes start to boil, throw in some chicken bouillon and butter.

Once the potatoes are halfway cooked, add chunks of onion, celery and cabbage. These cook so fast you'll need to time it right.

Now get a small bowl and mix a tablespoon or two of corn starch with milk, get it nice and mixed in before adding that to the pot. The corn starch thickens the gravy, but it's a bitch to mix in unless you get it blended with the milk really well.

Enjoy! Adding some bay leaves or lemon thyme improves the flavor, but I think it's pretty damn good all on it's open.

But where virtu is disciplined, it employs its ardor with moderation and at the right time; and no difficulty debases it, or makes it lose courage, because good order renews this courage and ardor, nourished by the hope of victory, which is never missing while discipline is preserved.

The contrary happens in those armies where there is ardor but no discipline; as were the Gauls, who were completely lacking in this while combatting, for if they did not succeed in winning with the first onset, in which they hoped, and not being sustained by a well regulated virtu, and not having anything outside of their fury in which to confide, they failed when that (first ardor) cooled.

The Romans were the opposite; they were less apprehensive of danger because of their good discipline, were not mistrusting of victory, fought with the same courage and virtu at the end as at the beginning (of a battle), the heat of battle actually inflaming them.
